summary: Describes what the IETF community expects Internet Service Providers to do about security, including how they should handle incidents, protect their own infrastructure, and cooperate with customers. It is a Best Current Practice and invites discussion and improvements.

eli5.summary: This is a safety checklist for the companies that connect you to the Internet, listing what good ones should do to keep their customers safe.

subtitle: What the IETF community hopes Internet service providers will do about security, from contact points to spoofing filters.

tldr.problem: Customers and other networks had no shared statement of what security behavior to expect from an Internet Service Provider (ISP).
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists recommended practices in four areas: communication, appropriate use policies, network infrastructure and systems infrastructure, using RFC 2119 words such as SHOULD and MUST NOT.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 46) that raises awareness and gives a framework for discussing security with current and prospective providers. It says it is not normative in its own right and may become dated.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The document states what the IETF engineering community expects of ISPs on security. It defines an ISP broadly, including web hosting, content and e-mail providers, but excludes organisations providing those services only for their own purposes.

It is addressed to ISPs, but it is deliberately modest. It does not set requirements suitable for every ISP and it does not dictate business practices. It also serves as advice to users about what to expect from a high quality provider. The text says it is in no sense normative in its own right and will likely become dated.
sections.eli5: It is a list of good habits that Internet companies are encouraged to have, not a set of strict rules.

sections.title: Communication and Incident Handling
sections.content:
The community's most significant expectations concern communication during security incidents. ISPs SHOULD follow RFC 2142, which defines the mailboxes SECURITY, ABUSE and NOC, and keep contact data in Whois and routing registries complete, accurate and reachable.

ISPs SHOULD have clear policies on sharing incident information with customers, other ISPs, response teams, law enforcement and the press, and SHOULD be able to communicate over a secure channel, though some jurisdictions may not permit this. They SHOULD proactively tell customers about vulnerabilities in their services and, during an incident, promptly report who is coordinating, the vulnerability, how service was affected, what is being done, whether customer data may be compromised, and the expected schedule if predictable.

ISPs should publish what incident response resources they offer, because a Computer Security Incident Response Team (CSIRT) may serve only paying subscribers. Customers are urged to learn this before an incident, using the CSIRT template from RFC 2350.
sections.eli5: If something goes wrong, you should know who to call at your Internet company, and they should tell you quickly and honestly what happened.

sections.title: Appropriate Use Policy
sections.content:
Every ISP SHOULD have an Appropriate Use Policy (AUP). Customer contracts should be governed by it, it should be reviewed at each renewal, and customers should be told proactively when it changes. It should state clearly what customers may and may not do, including the type of traffic allowed. For example, it might prohibit IP spoofing.

ISPs should publish the policy in a public place such as a web site, state which sanctions will be enforced, and consider data protection law, registering as a Data Controller where needed.
sections.eli5: It is like house rules for a shared pool: everyone should know what is allowed and what happens if you break the rules.

sections.title: Network Infrastructure
sections.content:
ISPs should manage their networks so they are reasonably resistant to known vulnerabilities and not easily hijacked for later attacks. Registry data, such as routing registry and regional registry entries, should only be updatable with strong authentication, and ISPs should register the address space they assign to customers.

Routing guidance: use BGP authentication (RFC 2385) with peers, take care whose announcements are trusted, and filter received routes, for example ignoring private address space and applying route flap damping (RFC 2439).

Two filters address forged source addresses. Ingress filtering at the boundary router drops customer traffic whose source is not an address assigned to that customer (see RFC 2827). Egress filtering drops traffic going to the customer that claims one of the customer's own addresses as its source. The RFC admits these are not always feasible, such as on large aggregation routers, and says filtering should be done as close to the hosts as possible.

Finally, routers on a broadcast medium MUST NOT be configured to allow directed broadcasts onto it (RFC 2644), since several denial of service attacks exploit them.
sections.eli5: Mail carriers should check that the return address on a letter really belongs to the sender, so nobody can pretend to be someone else.

sections.title: Systems Infrastructure
sections.content:
Different services such as mail, news and web hosting are easier to secure on separate systems. Critical systems SHOULD be reachable for management only by their administrators, after strong authentication and over an encrypted link, and only the ports of the services themselves should be reachable from outside. Systems should not be attached to transit network segments.

For e-mail, ISPs should prevent open mail relay used for Unsolicited Bulk E-mail (RFC 2505). Message submission should be authenticated with SMTP AUTH (RFC 2554), and submission is strongly recommended on port 587 (RFC 2476) rather than port 25, which can then be restricted to local delivery. The RFC says this also helps track accountability when a customer sends bulk mail.
sections.eli5: Lock the doors to the important rooms, give keys only to the people who work there, and make anyone who wants to send mail show who they are.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's own Security Considerations section is a single sentence: this entire document discusses security issues. The advice throughout is framed as recommendations that ISPs can adopt where appropriate, not as universal requirements.
sections.eli5: The whole document is about safety, so it has nothing extra to add here.
